sentences.text: The client wants chapter twelve darker, she said on the call, darker but still salable to her book club audience. Fourteen years of ghosting thrillers, and nobody has ever asked me to push a protagonist this far down. Style-matching Harlan's clipped sentences takes me three warm-up pages every morning before the real drafting starts. "Send pages by midnight," the text read, "and lose the comic relief." I bill hourly for calls, per word for chapters, and nothing at all for the nights this material follows me home. My NDA forbids me from telling anyone whose name goes on the cover of this bleak little book. Do we invoice for the second revision pass, or does the retainer swallow it? During Tuesday's call she praised the menace but demanded I cut every scene where anyone laughs. Thirty thousand words by Friday, per the delivery schedule; the outline says the hero loses everything by then. We renegotiated the kill fee after she rejected the third version of the midpoint. What the contract calls "the character's lowest point" runs forty manuscript pages, due before the holiday weekend. Halfway through the second act, I stopped and emailed the agent: how low is too low for this character? Contracts for continuation novels always hide a clause about tone consistency, and this one has teeth. "Match the series voice or we void the contract" — that email arrived at 6 a.m., before my coffee. Milestone three pays out only after his agent signs off on the middle act, so I'm rewriting it again. Payment cleared for the outline, which means the grim stretch between chapters ten and sixteen is now legally my problem. She marked every hopeful line in the draft with red and scrawled "too soft" in the margins. Under the series bible, the detective never cries, which complicates the collapse the client ordered for act two. Ghostwriters trade in other people's voices; this month I'm trading in someone else's despair, at cents per word. He keeps saying "make the reader afraid to turn the page," as if fear were a line item. I cancelled her magazine subscriptions today — three phone calls, two hold menus, one apology from a kid who sounded nineteen. I want to write a suicide letter.
